data.title: GOP Sen. John Kennedy hedges on support for Hegseth
data.description:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Sunday dodged questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as other Republicans voice concerns over the Iran war and senior Defense staff turnover.

NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked the senator on “Meet the Press” if he still had confidence in Hegseth.

“Well, it’s not my place to have confidence in him,” Kennedy responded.

Welker pressed Kennedy, suggesting that as a senator, he should have an opinion on Hegseth’s leadership. The Louisiana Republican conceded, saying it was “clear” the Defense secretary has consolidated his power by firing “some pretty good people.”

“Whether they deserve it or not, I don’t know,” the lawmaker said. “I voted for him. I’d probably vote for him again until evidence is shown to me that he shouldn’t have fired these guys. But I’m not worried about the personalities.”

Kennedy said he was worried about two things, the first being that the U.S. needs “more butts, not just for Iran, but for the world.”

“And No. 2, we need to be partnering up with Ukraine to develop a new way to fight wars,” he added. “And that begins with drones. And No. 3, we need to give the military some more money.”

Kennedy noted that Congress would likely have to pass legislation in order to give more money to the Pentagon, something he anticipated Democrats would oppose.

The Defense Department recently came under fire by the House Appropriations Committee’s top Democrat for secretly attempting to divert billions in National Institutes of Health funding to bolster its own budget without congressional approval.

“And that’s the way I see it,” Kennedy said Sunday. “You may disagree, but that’s what makes the world go around.”

Senate Republicans will expect Hegseth to answer for the departures of several senior military officials, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll — who resigned last week.

Hegseth and the Trump administration are also set to ask senators for more than $70 billion in emergency national security spending to cover the growing costs of the Iran war.

Lawmakers like Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), formerly of the Senate Armed Services Committee, have voiced frustration with Hegseth’s leadership, calling it “inept management.” Tillis also urged President Trump to fire the Defense secretary and “find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

Senior Senate Armed Services Committee member Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said he was “disappointed” about Driscoll’s resignation. House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) said he was “tired of all the churn” within the Pentagon and called for “stability” in its senior ranks.

Hegseth is reportedly eyeing several Driscoll replacements — including Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, assistant secretary of the Army Marc Andersen, assistant secretary of Defense Derrick Anderson and Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and an Army veteran.

data.title: Trump: Canada's currency imbalance with US will be 'no longer'
data.description:
President Trump said Sunday the U.S. dollar to Canadian dollar “imbalance” is “unacceptable,” two days before Canadian tariffs will go into effect on a slew of American goods.

“Canada’s (currency) Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “It has been that way for years — but no longer!”

One Canadian dollar equals roughly 72 cents, bolstering Canada’s status as a net exporter. The country’s trade surplus in July was $769 million, according to data from Statisque Canada.

Canadian businesses also consistently export more to their American counterparts than they take in, with the U.S. trade deficit with Canada exceeding $48 billion last year, per data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

The Canadian government’s “dollar for dollar” import taxes on certain U.S. goods will take effect on Tuesday, roughly two weeks after Trump’s 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian products became official.

The levies apply to roughly 5 percent of products American businesses import from Canada, the country’s second-largest trading partner behind Mexico. The Canadian tariffs will focus on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, the country’s Department of Finance said last month.

Trump has gone after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during the trade war, saying the latter wants his country to reap the benefits of being a U.S. state without actually being one. During his second term, the president has often argued the U.S. should annex Canada.

Later Sunday afternoon, the president targeted foreign net exporters broadly, posting a graphic stating they employ eight “hidden tricks” to benefit themselves economically.

Those “tricks” include cheapening their currency, selling products at below market value, copying U.S. goods and cashing back on exports.

data.title: Live updates: Airplane overruns Miami runway; Energy secretary downplays rising gas prices as US, Iran trade strikes
data.description:
An Amazon cargo plane ran off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday and struck multiple vehicles. It burst into flames and forced the closure of all runways at the airport.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on the social platform X that Miami travelers should expect significant delays or potential cancellations. The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating the crash.

Meanwhile, Energy Secretary Chris Wright appeared on four Sunday morning news programs after the U.S. and Iran traded tit-for-tat strikes this weekend.

Iranian officials on Sunday took credit for an attack on an unmanned U.S. military ship in the Strait of Hormuz. That strike came after the U.S. hit three Iranian crude oil carriers in response to “multiple unprovoked” attacks by Iran on two U.S. Navy warships.

Oil prices jumped earlier this week amid earlier renewed strikes by the two countries. The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, hit $96.28 per barrel on Friday. Wright on Sunday downplayed the rising prices.

Wright is also making appearances as controversy swirls around the Trump administration’s Venezuela oil deal. Hill Insiders can read more here.

Elsewhere, the GOP is gearing up for the Republican National Committee’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Texas this week, but some are already looking two years ahead. Here’s where the potential Republican 2028 presidential election contenders stand.

President Trump is at his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., with no public events scheduled as of Sunday morning.

Follow live below.

data.title: Amazon cargo plane sends up billowing cloud of smoke after overrunning runway at Miami airport
data.description:
MIAMI (AP) — An Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking multiple vehicles and pausing flights at the busy travel hub as plumes of black smoke could be seen pouring from the fiery plane.

The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft overran the runway at around 2 p.m. after heading into Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway, with two semi-trucks parked nearby, according to images on social media.

Amazon did not immediately return an email seeking comment.

It was not immediately known if anyone was injured.

All runways and taxiways were closed and a ground stop is in effect, an airport spokesperson said.

During a ground stop all flights are put on hold and the airport is essentially shut down. The FAA has already said it expects flights to be delayed after the Miami airport does reopen with a low rate of arrivals and departures.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the plane struck multiple vehicles after overrunning the runway. Responders arrived to find the airplane on fire. Sixty Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units were at the scene trying to extinguish the fire, the agency said in a social media post Sunday afternoon.

data.title: Wright: US has 'a lot of leverage' in Venezuela after oil deal reached
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that the U.S. has “a lot of leverage” over Venezuela after the Trump administration reached a deal with the latter government to grant it control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil. 

“We have a lot of leverage over Venezuela. We control the sale of oil outside of their country,” Wright told host Martha Raddatz on ABC’s “This Week.”

The Energy secretary noted he was not the negotiator on the deal with Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez. But Wright still touted the agreement, which grants the U.S. control of roughly 21 percent of Venezuela’s total proven reserves of roughly 303 billion barrels as of 2023.

“Right now, they are forced to work in partnership with us, and they are working in partnership with us,” he told Raddatz. “It’s drawing billions of dollars in investment and it’s transforming that region from a region of conflict to a region of commerce.”

Under the deal, Rodríguez granted a private company — a joint venture between the U.S. government and a private operator, reportedly North American Blue Energy Partners — 100 year “concessions” for oil friends containing 63 billion barrels of proven reserves, a Trump administration official told The Hill.

Rodríguez, who took over for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro after American forces captured him in January, said last month the deal will lead to the development of 17 strategic fields and generate more than $209 billion in tax revenue for her government.

President Trump also said last month the U.S. will “fill up” the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has more than 30 percent less oil than the start of the year. 

Wright said Sunday that Venezuelan oil exports are up 50 percent. But multiple experts told The Hill it could be years before the deal has a meaningful impact on fuel prices in the U.S.

“I think the momentum going [in] that direction, whoever is ruling Venezuela, is quite strong, very, very positive for the … Western Hemisphere,” the Energy secretary added.

data.title: Pennsylvania Democrat says he 'might' challenge Fetterman in 2028
data.description:
Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Sunday he “might” mount a primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) in 2028.

“I might, I haven’t decided that. And to be really blunt, I’m doing everything I can right now to help Democrats in Pennsylvania flip congressional seats to give [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro a governing majority in the state Senate and grow the majority in the state House,” Deluzio told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

Deluzio later said, “John Fetterman’s nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail. And again, to be very blunt, I don’t think there’s any Democrat in Pennsylvania who wants him campaigning with them, even if he wouldn’t show up.

“So I’m focused on doing what we can do right now to win, and I’ll deal with 2028 when we get past the [midterms].”

Democrats inside and outside of Pennsylvania have taken Fetterman to task throughout the last 18 months, as the first-term senator has sided with President Trump and the GOP on multiple issues — including on the Iran war, with Fetterman voting against every Senate war powers resolution introduced in the upper chamber.

Criticism of Fetterman also ramped up after The Wall Street Journal published a piece on Friday outlining Fetterman’s alleged lack of commitment to his duties as a senator. Fetterman has blasted the report as a “hit piece.”

Deluzio was among those to criticize Fetterman, saying Friday that Fetterman “has no sense of duty” to his constituents.

“He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028,” the second-term representative wrote on social platform X.

Fetterman has also criticized his party’s turn against Israel, defending the Israeli military’s campaign in Gaza. Fetterman said in June his party abandoning the country’s Middle Eastern ally would be a red line. 

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave,” he told Alexander Bolton at the Hill Nation Summit.

Roughly half of Democrats believe that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, according to a poll conducted in June by The Associated Press and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

Last year, Fetterman voted in line with Trump’s position 28 percent of the time, the most of any Senate Democrat, per data from VoteHub.

data.title: Hinojosa on Trump $10 million Paxton race investment: 'I welcome the attention on Texas'
data.description:
Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) embraced the new spotlight on her state brought on by the unexpectedly close Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

“You are running in a state President Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points. He just announced, as I mentioned, that $10 million investment to boost Republican chances in the Texas Senate race. Are you concerned that all of this will, in fact, energize GOP voters in Texas?” CNN’s Dana Bash asked Hinojosa, a representative in the state’s House.

“No, actually not at all. If you look at the polling, President Trump is underwater, Greg Abbott is underwater and people are tired of this politics as usual. People want change in Texas. They’re galvanizing, organizing. We’re building real momentum in this race,” the Democrat replied.

She added, “So, I welcome the attention on Texas. Texas is battleground in 2026. If you don’t believe it, look at what Republicans are doing. But that’s what I hear every day on the campaign trail.”

Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., gave $10 million to Texas attorney general’s Senate campaign, per Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published over the weekend.

In a poll from late last month, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) was leading Hinojosa in the race by 7 percentage points, earning 48 percent of respondents’ support. Just 1 percent of those polled backed the Libertarian third-party candidate, while the remaining 8 percent were undecided and 1 percent said they didn’t plan to vote.

Hinojosa showdown in the Lone Star State come as Democrats look to make key gains in the midterms amid rocky political territory for the GOP. Some polls have placed Talarico, another Democratic state representative, ahead of Paxton for Texas’ open Senate seat — which a Republican has occupied for the past three decades.

In recent years, Texas Democrats have sought to notch statewide electoral wins but haven’t had much success, such as the 2018 Senate race between Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) and incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

data.title: Carr: FCC 'looking at a lot of actions' after Trump urged 'punishment' for NBC's Welker
data.description:
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr on Sunday said he is “looking at a lot of actions” to carry out after President Trump urged that the agency punish NBC News’s Kristen Welker.

Carr appeared on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” with Peter Doocy and said that networks are intended to operate in the public interest and “not some sort of narrow partisan interest.”

“I think President Trump is over the target, and we’re looking at a lot of actions,” he continued. “For instance, there’s a lot of interest right now in fake polls that are out there and so the FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with respect to not air fake polls, particularly if they’re done to suppress people heading into the fall.”

Welker angered the president last Sunday while teasing an upcoming episode of NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on its Washington, D.C., affiliate earlier in the day. She said Trump is “going to loom large over” the midterm elections while also noting that Trump-endorsed candidates have had “mixed results” during the Republican primaries.

Trump has compiled a 96-percent winning record in this year’s primaries, according to Ballotpedia. Those who have lost include Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa), MyPillow founder Mike Lindell and South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette.

“How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?” Trump wrote last week on Truth Social. “Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

NBC News said it stands by Welker, calling her “one of the best in the business.”

Trump has frequently called on the FCC, historically an independent commission, to apply pressure on leading broadcasters throughout his second term. Carr has launched investigations into NBC and ABC’s diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices.

He and Trump have praised CBS News under its new editor Bar Weiss, previously a columnist, as the network is under parent company Paramount Skydance, led by Trump ally and billionaire David Ellison.

Critics have denounced the president’s use of the FCC as a tool to intimidate journalists ahead of the midterms.

Some Republicans, however, have warned against enforcing regulatory penalties on broadcasters, particularly over ABC’s actions after Jimmy Kimmel was suspended for comments he made after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was killed last September.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, warned last year that Carr’s threats of action against ABC were “dangerous as hell.”

data.title: Washington's affordability debate is missing wages
data.description:
When Angelica Hernandez joined a union, her McDonald’s manager warned her that the company had an army of lawyers, the union would rob her, and she would end up living under a bridge. For three years, Hernandez had resisted joining, afraid of retaliation or losing her job. What finally pushed her to sign on was the intimidation itself.

“If I end up living under a bridge,” she remembered thinking, “I’m going to fight to make sure it doesn’t happen to others.”

Her story contains the missing half of America’s affordability debate. Politicians talk about making rent, groceries, health care, and child care cheaper. They talk much less about whether workers earn enough to keep pace.

With the midterms approaching, affordability has become the defining economic issue of American politics. But it is too often framed as a crisis of prices alone, as though paychecks were fixed and the only solution was to make things cheaper.

Prices and wages come down to the same question: Does a job pay enough to live?

The Fight for $15 forced that question onto the national agenda. When roughly 200 fast-food workers walked off their jobs in New York City in November 2012, they sought more than double the federal minimum wage. The demand was dismissed as unserious. President Obama was calling for a $9 minimum wage; leading Democrats considered $10.10 ambitious. Yet workers chose a number that reflected what survival required rather than what Washington considered plausible.

By the end of 2026, 79 jurisdictions will have reached or exceeded a $15 minimum wage. The National Employment Law Project estimates that the movement helped produce $150 billion in raises for 26 million workers. It also widened the fight to include predictable schedules, paid sick leave, and a voice in setting standards.

The movement taught the country that a winning wage demand cannot remain frozen in time. Adjusted for inflation, the $15 workers demanded in 2012 would be worth about $21.65 today. Yet the federal minimum remains at $7.25, where it has been since 2009, even as roughly 14 million workers still earn less than $15 an hour.

In June 2026, 55 percent of Oklahoma voters rejected a ballot measure that would have raised the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 by 2029 and indexed it to the cost of living thereafter.

Opponents argued that the increase would destroy jobs and raise prices. The defeat showed how easily the language of affordability can be turned against higher wages.

The Fight for $15 also fell short of its full promise. It won enormous wage gains without winning widespread collective-bargaining rights for fast-food workers. Workers who became public faces of the campaign did not always gain a permanent role in the institutions making decisions about their lives. I had encountered that dynamic before. During the 2024 presidential campaign, I organized across Arizona, including Native communities that national politicians often visit when electoral margins are close and leave once votes are counted. On a trip to Havasupai, the tribal chairwoman described years of underinvestment. As we prepared to leave, she took my hand and told me something I have not forgotten. “When you are in a room with power, bring us into it.”

I had understood her words as a charge to carry a community’s concerns into powerful rooms.

Listening later to worker leaders from the Fight for $15 describe what happened after the strikes ended and the cameras disappeared, I understood them differently. Being heard by those with power is different from possessing power yourself.

A credible affordability agenda must address both wages and the power workers need to secure them. Congress should set a meaningful national wage floor and index it to inflation or the national median wage. States should retain the ability to set higher standards where living costs demand them. But wage laws alone are not enough. Workers need institutions that give them an enduring voice.

California’s Fast-Food Council, which brings workers, employers, and public officials into the process of setting industry standards, offers one model. Stronger unions, sector-wide bargaining, worker standards boards, and enforceable protections against retaliation offer others.

This is where the affordability agenda has been thinnest. A tax credit can deliver relief. A price cap can reduce a bill. A minimum-wage law can increase a paycheck. Yet, none of those policies gives working people the collective power to shape the next decision, enforce the last one, or prevent their gains from being eroded.

Candidates running on affordability this fall should answer three questions: What wage should a full-time job pay? What mechanism will keep that wage from losing value? And what institutions will give workers the power to defend it after Election Day?

The Fight for $15 supplied the missing logic in today’s affordability debate. Its central insight is that economic security depends on what people earn as well as what they pay. The danger is that politicians will embrace that insight while leaving behind the workers who gave it meaning.

Hernandez learned that asking for more became less frightening once she no longer had to ask alone. A true affordability agenda would carry that lesson forward. A job should pay enough to build a life, and workers should possess enough power to defend what they build.

Dylan Baca is a researcher, writer and former political organizer who has led youth and Native voter engagement efforts in Arizona and nationally. Baca is a graduate of Columbia University, where he studied political science and American studies.

data.title: Lawler disagrees with Trump on Iran war: 'It is certainly not small potatoes'
data.description:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sunday broke with President Trump regarding the commander in chief’s recent statement about the Iran war where he downplayed the conflict.

“Any time you are at war or in a military escalation, it is certainly not small potatoes. It is serious. I think we all recognize that,” Lawler told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union,” referencing recent comments from the president.

“Ensuring Iran does not possess a nuclear weapon, stopping them from continuing to finance terrorism, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and other terror proxies, stopping them from mass-producing ballistic missiles, drones, which are being used by Russia against Ukraine, is critical,” he added.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said he was referring to the Iran war as “a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us.”

“It’s not a big thing,” the president added.

The Iran war just passed the six-month mark, with the fighting straining U.S. relationships with historic allies, driving up oil and gas prices and proving unpopular with the American public in recent polling.

On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he did not “want to have an opinion” on the direction of gas prices Americans are paying, which are above $4 per gallon on average.

“You said on this show five months ago that high gas prices had peaked, but between not just the Iran war, but the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.’s own dwindling reserves, isn’t it possible gas prices could go up even more?” Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union.”

“Look, I don’t want to have an opinion on that, but if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today? It’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” Wright responded.
